query: More than a century of research on conventional steels and other alloys has shown that exposure within certain temperature ranges can sharply reduce toughness and threaten safety in aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical applications. High-entropy alloys offer attractive strength, ductility, resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement, and wear resistance; however, their multicomponent chemistry complicates predictions of long-term mechanical reliability. Their resistance to rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation does not establish whether their toughness will remain stable after service-relevant heating, and this uncertainty limits engineering use. For a high-performance multicomponent high-entropy alloy in its as-designed condition, under the constraint that its original strength–ductility combination must be retained, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to reduce post-exposure toughness degradation? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to an otherwise identical untreated baseline, define the temperature, duration, and loading boundaries, identify supporting evidence from the observations summarized above, and describe a decisive experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a small amount of tungsten carbide (WC) to a high-entropy alloy (HEA) will reduce post-exposure toughness degradation after service-relevant heating.
generation.intervention: Addition of a small amount of tungsten carbide (WC)
generation.conditions: Service-relevant heating, with temperature range between 600°C to 1000°C, and duration of 100 hours
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable solid solution structure with dispersed WC particles
generation.mechanism: The dispersed WC particles will act as obstacles to dislocation movement, reducing the formation of deleterious intermetallic phases and grain coarsening, thus maintaining the alloy's toughness
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced post-exposure toughness degradation, with a predicted toughness retention of at least 80% compared to the untreated baseline
generation.baseline: Untreated high-entropy alloy with the same composition and processing history
generation.boundary: Temperature range between 600°C to 1000°C, duration of 100 hours, and loading conditions of up to 500 MPa
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of WC required to achieve the desired effect, and the potential for other factors such as oxidation or corrosion to influence the outcome

falsification_experiment.design: Comparison of the toughness of WC-added HEA and untreated HEA after service-relevant heating, using a combination of mechanical testing and microstructural analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the WC-added HEA shows no significant improvement in toughness retention compared to the untreated HEA, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys consist of alloying elements with five or more equal molar fractions, each of which has a molar fraction of about 5% to 35%. As a kind of comprehensive material, high entropy alloy has better physical and chemical properties than many common metal compounds []. Therefore, it has attracted wide attention in material science and engineering and is the focus field of scholars at home and abroad [,]. In recent years, many scholars at home and abroad have used high entropy alloys for surface modification, mainly by laser melting, laser deposition, and plasma melting. The lower preparation cost and excellent performance of high entropy alloys not only improve their service life and significantly reduce the failure loss but also reduce their surface repair cost, and high entropy alloys have many advantages that traditional alloys can hardly match []. However, there are difficulties in the synergistic enhancement of strength, toughness, and corrosion resistance of high entropy alloys, and no satisfactory solution has been found so far []. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) constitute one of the most innovative classes of metallic materials, attracting significant attention from both scientific and industrial communities in recent years [,,]. Their uniqueness lies in the design of chemical composition, where several principal elements are present in nearly equimolar proportions, leading to the formation of high-entropy phases with simplified crystalline structures [,]. These materials exhibit exceptional mechanical, thermal, and corrosion resistance properties, often surpassing those of traditional engineering alloys [,]. HEAs, particularly the Cantor alloy (CoCrFeMnNi), remain among the most recognized and extensively studied representatives within this group []. Since its discovery, the Cantor alloy has attracted significant scientific attention due to its exceptional mechanical properties, distinguishing it from both conventional and other HEAs [,]. It exhibits a single-phase FCC structure with excellent ductility and resistance to brittle fracture, even under cryogenic conditions [,,]. The concept of high entropy alloy (HEA) was proposed and published in 2004 [,,] and the unique properties of these alloys have attracted attention from research groups all over the world. The pioneering studies by Cantor et al. were the first to report that an equiatomic alloy consisting of the five transition metals Cr, Mn, Fe, Co and Ni crystallized as a single solid solution [,] in the as-cast and in the homogenized state. The first HEA generation could contain five or more main elements with the concentration of each element in the range 5–35 at. % []. The alloys presented a high mixing entropy in their liquid state [] and thus could form simple solid solution structures (e.g., FCC, BCC and HCP) in place of intermetallic phases. Some promising technological characteristics of HEAs were high hardness [], good wear resistance [], excellent strength at both high and low temperatures [,,] and generally a good resistance to oxidation and corrosion [].
